meta.title: Zulu B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 778 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Zulu → English (see the Zulu, recall the meaning) and English → Zulu (see an English meaning, recall the Zulu). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 778 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Zulu, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 59 of the 778 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the everyday phrases and exclamations, the phone, the office and work, dressing, food and the table, the household and its chores, health, the town, feelings and character, talking, time and cost, and the weather — and the other 719 are the commonest remaining words of the Zulu Wikipedia, counted by the WHOLE word: Zulu joins its prefixes to the word (abantu, kumuntu, ngiyahamba), so every form of a noun or a verb is added together. That corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (history, government, sport). The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here, and a few everyday words are missing from it (kodwa 'but', namuhla 'today', nini 'when'). A noun is shown whole with its NOUN CLASS — the prefix family that every adjective, verb and pronoun agreeing with it echoes; the Zulu Noun Classes deck, first in this collection, teaches them — and its plural and locative ('at, in, to'): 468 nouns here. A verb, an adjective or a relative is shown by its stem with a hyphen (-hamba, -khulu), as Zulu dictionaries print it, since none stands without a prefix; the 269 verbs give their infinitive and plural command, and behind the Tenses fold their present, negative, past and future by person, taken from Wiktionary's own tables. Beneath each headword is Wiktionary's tone-marked spelling (umúntu, -hámba): ordinary Zulu writing marks no tone, but the language has it. Example sentences are few: 14 of the 778 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about a hundred Zulu sentences; none is invented. A speaker reads the word and each sentence where the device has a Zulu voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, noun classes, forms, tables and tones: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Zulu Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
